## Provisional Shop Recommendation {.unnumbered}

For a shop system intended to observe fast whole-body motion and eventually use six to eight
cameras, the current evidence supports a **two-camera pilot**, not an immediate full-rig purchase.
The provisional first candidate is the color Teledyne FLIR Blackfly S
`BFS-U3-16S2C-CS`; the Basler ace 2 `a2A1920-160ucBAS` is the matched alternate.
Both are global-shutter industrial cameras with hardware-trigger support and replaceable lenses.
The FLIR candidate trades resolution for a higher vendor-specified maximum rate (226 frames per
second at 1440 by 1080 in BayerRG8 with a 10-bit ADC setting); Basler documents 164 frames per
second at its default 1920-by-1200 settings. Resolution, pixel format, exposure and firmware must
be recorded together: a model name or headline maximum is not a complete acquisition mode.

The distributed eight-camera reference-rig evaluation hypothesis remains the Allied Vision Alvium
G5-203 (`Alvium G5-203c`), with the LUCID Triton2 `TRT016S-CC` as an Ethernet/PTP challenger.
These distributed candidates operate over 5GigE and 2.5GigE Vision with IEEE 1588 PTP synchronization,
addressing the cabling and host-controller bottlenecks of high-rate USB topologies across large
capture volumes.

The Stereolabs ZED X One GS remains an evaluation candidate for spaces where synchronized
GMSL2 cabling is valuable. It is not the default fast-motion choice: its full-resolution mode is
60 frames per second, its 120-frame-per-second mode is binned to 960 by 600, its vendor dual-camera
hardware synchronization claim is 15 microseconds, and the complete topology adds capture-card,
NVIDIA, fixed-lens, and SDK-version constraints.

This recommendation is deliberately provisional. Camera specifications alone cannot establish
pose, joint-angle, or C3D accuracy. A successful two-camera USB pilot does not establish an
eight-camera distributed topology, and an attractive camera-body specification does not qualify the
complete lab. First define the intended output and its error budget, obtain comparable quotes,
and qualify a matched pair. Evaluate distributed Ethernet candidates separately for the full room.
A conditional decision to buy two cameras for the pilot requires the lens, host and software review
below; no candidate has already earned that decision through a physical test.

::: {.callout-warning title="No Procurement Approval & Price Scoping"}
No listed camera is approved for a full deployment. The earlier camera-body price observations
are historical, not current quotes. Current comparable regional prices are unavailable.
Complete system costs remain unavailable until formal quotes include lenses, GPIO/trigger
hardware, host controllers, topology-specific power/network equipment, cabling, mounting, lighting, storage,
spares, taxes, and shipping. The machine-readable registry defaults procurement to deny.
:::

## Governed Evidence

The canonical dataset is the
[camera evidence registry](../data/markerless_mocap/camera_evidence_registry_v1.json). Its schema is
`affinedrift/mocap-camera-evidence-registry/v1`, and
`scripts/verify_mocap_camera_registry.py` rejects missing sources, review dates expired relative to the registry date, unknown source IDs,
cross-camera claim ownership, incomplete purchasing attributes, and status inconsistencies.
Those checks establish structural consistency; they cannot establish that a source supports a value.
The incorrect camera modes corrected in this review previously passed those checks.

Evidence classes have intentionally different authority:

| Evidence Class | What It Can Establish | What It Cannot Establish |
|---|---|---|
| `vendor_spec` | A vendor's dated statement about its product or SDK | Sustained rig performance or independent accuracy |
| `peer_reviewed_observed` | What a cited study observed under its own protocol | Transfer to another camera, task, pose model, or lab |
| `engineering_inference` | A transparent design screen or pilot decision | A qualified threshold or procurement approval |
| `unavailable` | That the necessary value is not currently authoritative | A value to be silently estimated or substituted |

AffineDrift owns this public evidence and explanation only. Tools owns camera, time, frame,
calibration, and interchange contracts. UpstreamDrift owns capture orchestration, calibration
execution, reconstruction, validation, and operator workflows. This page does not implement or
duplicate either runtime.

### Teledyne FLIR Fast-Motion Pilot Candidate

The FLIR candidate leads the two-camera pilot because temporal sampling is the first screen for rapid
motion. The vendor lists a global shutter, 226 frames per second at full 1440-by-1080 BayerRG8 output with 10-bit ADC, a
CS-mount lens interface, and hardware trigger support. The separate I/O documentation describes the
physical input and its propagation specification. None of these statements proves exposure alignment
between two assembled cameras, reliable eight-camera streaming, or pose accuracy.

The cited [Spinnaker agreement](https://intecore.teledynevisionsolutions.com/globalassets/support/iis/knowledge-base/flir-spinnaker-sdk-eula-2018.pdf)
contains camera-use restrictions and separate terms for open-source components. It does not
establish the license of a future SDK build or change the license of the open core. A camera adapter must remain optional and satisfy the public Tools camera protocol. Synthetic
and prerecorded drivers must continue to work when Spinnaker is absent.

### Basler Higher-Resolution Alternate

The Basler candidate offers 2.3 megapixels at 164 frames per second under default settings, global shutter, C-mount optics, a
hardware-trigger input, and GenICam-facing pylon APIs. Its additional pixels may improve keypoint
localization when the person occupies a smaller portion of the image; that possible benefit is an
inference to test, not a result. The lower maximum frame rate may be immaterial for some body segments
and insufficient for others.

The pylon SDK is also governed by a vendor license. It belongs behind an optional adapter. A commercial
release must review the exact pylon license shipped with the chosen SDK version rather than relying on
this summary.

### Stereolabs Long-Cable Evaluation

The ZED X One GS offers a synchronized, locking GMSL2 topology and fixed narrow or wide GS lens variants. Stereolabs
technical documentation states that dual ZED X One hardware synchronization is accurate to **15 microseconds**,
and multi-device ZED Box documentation states approximately **15 microseconds**. This makes the system
interesting where USB cable length and connector reliability dominate. It does not remove the need to
measure exposure timing, transport drops, or model latency on the assembled system.

The comparison must preserve mode context. `120 frames per second` applies to the 960-by-600 binned mode,
while full 1920-by-1200 output is limited to 60 frames per second. A pair is required for ZED SDK stereo
or depth features. The SDK and capture topology depend on supported NVIDIA hardware, and their licenses
and redistribution terms remain separate review gates.

### Allied Vision Distributed Reference-Rig Hypothesis

The Alvium G5-203c remains an Ethernet candidate, with a Sony IMX422 global-shutter sensor,
1632-by-1248 output, 5GBASE-T and PoE. Its model-specific datasheet lists 225 fps at a
525-MByte/s setting in Mono8. Treat that mode condition as part of the specification, including
for this color variant. The datasheet lists hardware triggering, action commands and PTP.

Longer Ethernet runs can simplify placement, subject to the selected cable, connectors and
vendor link qualification. A 5-Gbit/s interface is a capacity, not the traffic of every mode.
Size each shared link, switch egress, host bus and recording path from the actual payload and
measured overhead. Synchronized acquisition may create bursts even when average traffic fits.

Vimba X is the vendor SDK. Its [licensing information](https://docs.alliedvision.com/legalInformation.html)
identifies vendor terms and component licenses. Preserve the optional adapter boundary and
review the exact deployed components; protocol compatibility alone does not grant redistribution rights.

### LUCID Triton2 Distributed Ethernet Challenger

The LUCID Triton2 `TRT016S-CC` provides an Ethernet/PTP challenger for the distributed reference rig.
Its Sony IMX273 global-shutter sensor provides 1440-by-1080 output at a stated maximum of
166.3 fps, with 2.5GBASE-T, PoE and PTP. The vendor states a 10% device-link reserve for resend;
record the actual pixel format and reserve in the capture configuration.

The previous 226-fps claim was incorrect: even uncompressed eight-bit pixels would need
2.812 Gbit/s, exceeding 2.5 Gbit/s before overhead. A slower link does not reduce the bytes of
a fixed acquisition mode or guarantee lower CPU load. The [Arena SDK](https://thinklucid.com/arena-software-development-kit/)
provides vendor camera APIs and GenICam access; verify the intended integration path and
release-specific license rather than assuming a GenTL producer or redistribution permission.

## Topology Comparison

| Parameter | Two-Camera USB Pilot | Distributed Ethernet Reference Rig | Long-Cable GMSL2 Rig |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Representative Models** | FLIR BFS-U3-16S2C-CS, Basler a2A1920-160ucBAS | Allied Vision Alvium G5-203c, LUCID Triton2 TRT016S-CC | Stereolabs ZED X One GS |
| **Physical Transport** | USB 3.0 / USB 3.1 Gen 1 | 5GBASE-T / 2.5GBASE-T Ethernet (PoE) | GMSL2 with FAKRA connectors |
| **Cable Qualification** | Qualify the exact passive or active cable and controller | Qualify cable category, length, connector and link speed | Qualify camera, coax cable and capture-card combination |
| **Synchronization** | Compatible common hardware trigger; measure exposure skew | PTP clock alignment plus verified trigger/scheduling support | Vendor 15 µs hardware-sync claim for supported topology |
| **Power Distribution** | USB bus power (host controller dependent) | Power-over-Ethernet (802.3af/at switch) | Power over Coax / capture card |
| **Host Interface** | Qualified controller groups and host buses | NICs and switches sized for aggregate traffic | Supported deserializer/capture hardware and compute |
| **Driver Interface** | Qualified Spinnaker or pylon adapter | Qualified Vimba X or Arena adapter | Supported ZED SDK or lower-level driver path |
| **Lab Role** | Initial fast-motion screening (2 cameras) | Full-room distributed rig (8 cameras) | Fixed-lens long-cable evaluation |

## Scoped Pricing vs Total System Cost

Earlier records contained USD 371 for FLIR and USD 399/424 for ZED camera bodies. Those
observations are not current offers. On rechecking, the FLIR listing showed a different dollar
amount and the old ZED store URL redirected without a matching configuration price. The registry
now marks current regional prices unavailable and preserves the historical amounts only in its
limitations. Obtain dated, configuration-specific quotes for all five candidates.

A complete mocap lab requires extensive infrastructure beyond the camera body:

1. **Optics**: High-resolution C/CS-mount lenses with manual focus/aperture locks with a dated quote for the chosen lens.
2. **Synchronization & I/O**: Shielded trigger breakout cables, opto-isolated distribution amplifiers, or a qualified PTP topology; a separate grandmaster is not universally required.
3. **Cabling**: High-flex locking USB cables, Cat6A shielded Ethernet cables, or FAKRA GMSL2 cables.
4. **Host & Ingest**: Multi-channel PCIe host controllers, multi-Gigabit PoE switches, dedicated NVMe scratch arrays.
5. **Mounting & Structure**: Rigid wall/truss mounts, vibration dampeners, protective enclosures.
6. **Illumination**: High-CRI flicker-free LED lighting panels.
7. **Spares & Logistics**: Cold spares, shipping, regional import tariffs, and taxes.

Complete system cost comparisons remain unavailable until comprehensive, dated bills of materials are
quoted for each candidate topology.

## Selection Calculations

### Temporal Sampling

For locally constant image speed $v_{px}$ in pixels per second and a camera rate $f_s$, the nominal
inter-frame displacement is

$$
\Delta p = \frac{v_{px}}{f_s}.
$$ {#eq-inter-frame-displacement}

For varying motion, displacement is the integral of image velocity over the actual frame
interval; the expression is a local screen. It is not a Nyquist criterion or an impact-duration
measurement. Pixel speed must be evaluated after choosing field of view and resolution.
This equation does not choose a universal frame rate. Measure $v_{px}$ for the intended body,
club, implement, or tool region, then set a task-specific maximum displacement. A body-pose model
may tolerate a displacement that is unacceptable for a fast implement. The registry's
120-frame-per-second pilot screen is therefore provisional.

### Motion Blur

If exposure time is $t_e$, the approximate image-space motion blur is

$$
b_{px} = v_{px} t_e.
$$ {#eq-motion-blur}

For a declared blur budget $b_{max}$, the exposure contract is

$$
t_e \leq \frac{b_{max}}{v_{px}}.
$$ {#eq-exposure-contract}

A high frame rate does not automatically create a short exposure. Lighting, aperture, gain,
sensor response, and flicker determine whether the required exposure is usable. A global shutter
aligns rows within an image but does not eliminate motion blur or synchronize different cameras. The pilot must
record exposure, gain, illumination, and observed blur for every camera.

### Raw Payload Screen

An uncompressed payload screen for width $W$, height $H$, frame rate $f_s$, and delivered bit
depth $q$ is

$$
R_{raw} = W H f_s q.
$$ {#eq-raw-payload}

Here $q$ is the **delivered bits per pixel**, including color channels and packing, not the ADC
setting. Bayer8 uses 8 bits (one byte) per pixel; RGB8 uses 24 bits (three bytes). A 12-bit sample stored in a 16-bit
container consumes two bytes; packed 12-bit output uses 1.5 bytes before row padding. Debayering
on the host increases downstream memory traffic even when the camera link carries Bayer8.
Use the driver's actual payload size when chunks, padding or compression are present.

| Arithmetic Screen | Pixels and Rate | One Stream (Gbit/s) | Eight Streams (Gbit/s) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| FLIR BayerRG8, 10-bit ADC | 1440 × 1080 at 226 fps | 2.812 | 22.494 |
| Basler eight-bit default-region screen | 1920 × 1200 at 164 fps | 3.023 | 24.183 |
| Allied datasheet Mono8 condition | 1632 × 1248 at 225 fps | 3.666 | 29.329 |
| LUCID eight-bit maximum-rate screen | 1440 × 1080 at 166.3 fps | 2.069 | 16.552 |

These are decimal payload rates, excluding transport overhead, resend, file headers and copies.
They are not measured sustained modes. In particular, confirm the Basler and LUCID format/rate
combination at the driver, and do not transfer Allied's Mono8 rate to RGB8. FLIR's own table
reduces full-resolution BayerRG8 from 226 to 165 fps when its ADC changes from 10 to 12 bits.
An eight-camera Allied screen needs about 3.666 GB/s of image storage before overhead; interface
capacity, PCIe sharing, buffer bursts and sustained disk writes all require separate checks.

Ethernet is one possible architecture, not a requirement imposed by camera count. Independent
USB controller groups or multiple acquisition hosts are alternatives if the complete timing and
throughput contract passes. Conversely, one nominal 10GbE uplink cannot carry the eight-camera
payloads above uncompressed at these rates. A topology diagram must identify every shared bottleneck.

The acquisition contract must measure successful payload, dropped and duplicate frames, buffer
occupancy, host-controller/NIC assignment, CPU load, storage write rate, and graceful recovery. A
nominal interface bandwidth label is not a per-camera end-to-end guarantee.

### Clock Alignment, Exposure Timing and Reconstruction

PTP aligns clocks. A common hardware trigger or supported scheduled action determines when
acquisition begins; trigger latency and exposure duration then determine the image's effective
time. Packet arrival time is a different quantity. [LUCID's synchronization example](https://support.thinklucid.com/app-note-multi-camera-synchronization-using-ptp-and-scheduled-action-commands/)
configures PTP and trigger actions separately, and schedules transfer to manage bursts. That
example uses other models; confirm equivalent nodes and firmware on the candidate TRT016S-CC.

For uniform integration during locally constant motion, use the exposure midpoint as a first
approximation to image time. Two equal start times with unequal exposures have unequal midpoints.
At image speed $v_{px}$ and midpoint mismatch $\delta t$, the correspondence displacement is
approximately $|v_{px}\delta t|$. Clock offset, clock drift, trigger jitter and exposure timing
must therefore be measured separately under load. A timing figure is not itself a 3D error bound.

For an explicitly illustrative $10{,}000$ pixels/s point, 200 fps gives 50 pixels between frames;
100 microseconds exposure gives approximately one pixel of blur; 50 microseconds midpoint skew
gives approximately half a pixel of cross-view mismatch. Increasing frame rate fixes neither of
the latter two quantities automatically. A 40 m/s point travels 0.6 mm in 15 microseconds, but
triangulation may amplify that inconsistency and motion direction matters. These are constructed
examples, not measurements of a golfer or any camera.

### Triangulation Geometry

For calibrated, rectified stereo with parallel optical axes, focal length $f$ in pixels,
baseline $B$ and positive horizontal disparity $d$, the ideal pinhole relation is

$$
z=\frac{fB}{d}, \qquad
\sigma_z\approx\frac{z^2}{fB}\sigma_d.
$$ {#eq-depth-sensitivity}

This is a first-order standard-deviation estimate with fixed calibration and small disparity
error. If left and right localization errors $e_L,e_R$ have standard deviations $\sigma_L,\sigma_R$,
then $\sigma_d^2=\sigma_L^2+\sigma_R^2-2\operatorname{Cov}(e_L,e_R)$.
Equal independent errors give $\sigma_d=\sqrt{2}\sigma_{px}$; correlated errors do not.
With $f=1000$ pixels, $B=1$ m, $z=4$ m and independent 0.5-pixel errors, the estimate is
11.3 mm. A positive ten-pixel disparity bias instead changes the reconstructed depth from 4 m
to approximately 3.846 m. Random localization precision and systematic timing bias are distinct.

For arbitrary camera placement, linearize the actual calibrated projections. If $J$ maps a
3D point perturbation to stacked image-coordinate perturbations and image covariance $\Sigma_u$
is positive definite, a locally identifiable weighted least-squares point estimate has

$$
\Sigma_X\approx\left(J^\mathsf{T}\Sigma_u^{-1}J\right)^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-multiview-covariance}

This conditional estimate requires full column rank and a valid local noise model. Include
calibration uncertainty and timing parameters in a joint model or propagate them separately;
the formula alone omits them. Near-parallel rays make depth poorly conditioned. Wider baselines
can improve geometry while increasing occlusion and appearance differences. More cameras help
only when their observations add usable information; repeated biased detections are not
independent evidence. Detector confidence is not automatically a calibrated variance.

### From Image Error to Golf-Swing Inference

Camera selection affects the argument we can make about a swing. Exposure blur changes landmark
localization; timing mismatch combines different poses; calibration and view geometry transform
those image errors into anisotropic 3D errors. Fitting a skeleton adds joint definitions,
anthropometry and constraints. Filtering trades noise against temporal detail and may shift
estimated events. A smooth reconstruction can therefore hide uncertainty rather than remove it.

Differentiation is especially sensitive. For independent zero-mean position noise with standard
deviation $\sigma_X$ in one coordinate, sampled every $\Delta t$, the unfiltered central-difference
velocity and acceleration noise are

$$
\sigma_v=\frac{\sigma_X}{\sqrt{2}\Delta t}, \qquad
\sigma_a=\frac{\sqrt{6}\sigma_X}{\Delta t^2}.
$$ {#eq-differentiation-noise}

At 200 Hz and $\sigma_X=1$ mm, these are about 0.141 m/s and 98.0 m/s². These values describe
those stencils and an independent-noise model, not a calibrated mocap system. Correlated noise
and filtering change the result. They explain why a position error acceptable for visualization
may be unacceptable for acceleration or a brief sequencing claim.

Finally, inverse dynamics needs acceleration, segment inertial properties and external loads
in addition to pose. Camera data alone do not uniquely measure muscle forces or identify neural
commands. State which load measurements, contact assumptions and regularization supply missing
information. Validate positions, joint definitions, derivatives and force estimates at their
own level before using them to argue for a mechanism of the golf swing.

## What the Research Establishes

[Nakano and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2020.00050) evaluated five synchronized
cameras at 1920 by 1080 and 120 hertz and reported task- and keypoint-dependent markerless error.
Its two participants performed walking, jumping and throwing; it also tested 3840-by-2160
video at 30 Hz. Resolution and rate changed together, so this is not an isolated frame-rate
experiment. The study does not qualify any industrial camera or golf-swing endpoint here.

[OpenCap](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011462) used 720-by-1280 smartphone videos at 60 hertz and synchronized
keypoints in processing using cross-correlations of their velocities. This is software temporal
alignment, not evidence of hardware-synchronized exposure. It is an important accessible baseline,
not evidence that 60 hertz is sufficient for every shop task or that its accuracy transfers to a
different camera, detector, skeleton, or calibration pipeline.

[Song and colleagues](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37552921/) compared markerless and
marker-based estimates across eight movements and reported larger hip differences, especially for rapid movement such as running, in ten
participants. That abstract-level observation does not establish a universal speed-error law.
Agreement with marker-based estimates also is not proof of absolute anatomical accuracy. This reinforces a central rule: qualification is
task-, joint-, model-, and protocol-specific.

## Two-Camera Pilot Protocol

1. Obtain complete quotes for two FLIR cameras and two comparable Basler cameras. Include matched
   lenses, locking data cables, isolated trigger distribution, mounts, tripods or structure,
   lights, host controllers, storage, taxes, shipping, and one spare strategy.
2. Review the exact SDK versions and EULAs. The MIT core must operate without either vendor SDK.
3. Select lenses from the measured capture-volume dimensions. Record field of view, working
   distance, focus, aperture, and distortion; do not select only by nominal focal length.
4. Bench two matched cameras at the intended resolution, bit depth, frame rate, exposure, and
   cable length. Measure exposure skew, drift, frame loss, duplicates, jitter, and recovery.
5. Calibrate a real two-camera geometry, retain every observation and solver version, and report
   residuals, covariance, ray-angle coverage, and movement invalidation.
6. Run the intended pose backend on representative clothing, lighting, occlusion, body sizes,
   and motions. Keep detector confidence separate from geometric uncertainty.
7. Compare triangulated points and derived joint quantities against a declared reference. Report
   all unavailable and failed keypoints; never interpolate them silently.
8. Repeat at the worst intended capture-volume locations. If the intended output includes club
   motion, derivatives or dynamics, validate those outputs and their required load/model inputs
   as well as body pose. Only then compare rate and resolution against the declared task budget.
9. Add cameras in stages. Re-run synchronization, bandwidth, calibration, visibility, thermal,
   storage, and pose tests before scaling to an eight-camera distributed topology.

## Required Qualification Evidence

The full-rig decision remains blocked until the following evidence exists:

- a dated bill of materials and exact license review;
- a camera capability record from the real driver rather than a product-name switch;
- sustained stream results at every supported camera count and mixed-capability case;
- exposure timing for the chosen trigger/clock architecture, plus drift, drop, duplicate, and recovery measurements;
- intrinsic and extrinsic calibration observations, residuals, covariance, and validity state;
- task-volume visibility and ray-angle maps with occlusion and lighting challenges;
- reference comparisons for the actual pose model, skeleton, filtering, and biomechanical outputs;
- C3D export and independent-reader round trips with units, rates, residuals, events, and explicit
  loss reporting;
- privacy, consent, retention, security, SBOM, and redistribution approval; and
- an exact-version commissioning report that states what the rig cannot measure.

## Extension Contract

A new camera does not require a core code change when it satisfies the shared provider protocol.
Its adapter must report capabilities such as stream modes, shutter, trigger, clocks, controls,
pixel formats, lens metadata, and cancellation. Unsupported functions return typed unsupported
outcomes. The lab manifest selects providers and records immutable device identities and settings;
the reconstruction code consumes canonical observations and never switches behavior by vendor
name.

To add a camera to this public registry, add its dated primary sources, exactly one claim for every
purchasing attribute, limitations, review dates, and an explicit adapter state. If price, sync,
license, or topology is unknown, record `unavailable`. The verifier will reject an apparently
complete camera assembled from missing or cross-model claims.

## Current Limitations

- No candidate has been connected to this workstation under the canonical Tools protocol.
- No physical timing, blur, lighting, field-of-view, pose, triangulation, or C3D test has run.
- Complete system costs remain unavailable until comparable complete regional quotes exist.
- Vendor SDK summaries are not legal opinions.
- The cited studies bound only their own cameras, participants, models, tasks, and protocols.
- This document does not approve human-subject recording, public release, or biomechanical use.

Begin with a declared measurement target and complete quotes. Select a matched pilot pair only
after its mode, optics, timing, software and host requirements are supportable; expand after
the measured results satisfy that target. No specification table can substitute for this chain.
